questions.question: In polynomial long division, what are $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ called?
options: The leading term and the constant term

questions.question: What degree condition must the remainder satisfy after dividing by $b(x)$?
Why is the divisor $b(x)$ required to be nonzero?
options: The remainder would always have degree $0$
The quotient would always be zero
Division by the zero polynomial is not defined
Only zero divisors have unique quotients

questions.question: What integer-arithmetic idea is polynomial long division analogous to?
What does uniqueness mean in polynomial long division?
options: The remainder must always be zero
There is only one polynomial in the field.
The quotient and remainder are fixed by $a(x)$ and $b(x)$.

questions.question: Dividing $x^2-1$ by $x-1$ gives which quotient and remainder?
Divide $x^2+1$ by $x+1$. What is the remainder?
When dividing by $x-3$, what degree can the remainder have?
options: The same degree as the dividend

questions.question: Which identity correctly expresses division of $a(x)$ by $b(x)$?
If $a(x)=(x+2)b(x)$, what is the remainder when $a(x)$ is divided by $b(x)$?
Why does the condition $\deg r \lt \deg b$ matter?
options: It forces the divisor to be linear
It makes the quotient always constant.
It makes the remainder smaller than the divisor.
It makes every polynomial have a root

questions.question: Why is a field used as the coefficient system for polynomial long division?
options: Leading coefficients need division by nonzero scalars.
Fields are needed only to count roots
A field makes every remainder zero

questions.question: What does a zero remainder tell us about $a(x)$ and $b(x)$?
Divide $x^3-1$ by $x-1$. What is the quotient?
Divide $x^2+3x+5$ by $x+1$. What is the quotient and remainder?
If dividing $a(x)$ by a quadratic $b(x)$ gives a nonzero remainder, which form is possible for the remainder?
Why does uniqueness rule out two different nonzero remainders of degree below $\deg b$?
options: The quotient is unique but the remainder is not
Uniqueness holds only when the divisor is constant.
Remainders are allowed to be arbitrary polynomials
A unique quotient-remainder pair satisfies the degree condition.

questions.question: What distinguishes exact divisibility from general polynomial division?
options: Exact divisibility requires the divisor to be zero.
It is the case of zero remainder.
General division is only possible over integers.

questions.question: Divide $2x^3+x^2-5x+2$ by $x-1$. What is the remainder?
If $a(x)=q(x)b(x)+r(x)$, $\deg b=3$, and $r(x)=x^3+1$, what is wrong?
options: The remainder degree is not less than $\deg b$.
The dividend must equal the remainder.
